World.title: KazMunayGas reviews progress of major oil and gas chemical projects in Atyrau
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. Chairman of the Management Board of Kazakhstan's national oil and gas company KazMunayGas (KMG) Askhat Khassenov reviewed the progress of major oil and gas chemical projects during a working visit to the Atyrau region, KMG said.

Khassenov visited the construction site of the Silleno polyethylene plant, which is designed to produce 1.25 million tons of polyethylene per year.

The project is preparing for the installation of its first large-scale piece of equipment - a fractionation column for the pyrolysis unit. Manufactured by Kazakhstan's AtyrauNefteMash plant, the column is 101.8 meters high, 7.5 meters in diameter and weighs about 1,500 tons.

A crawler crane with a maximum lifting capacity of 4,000 tons has been delivered to the Atyrau region for the installation works.

Overall progress on the Silleno project has reached 36%. Foundation works for buildings, equipment and pipe racks at the pyrolysis unit are 57% complete, while pile driving and foundation works at the polymerization unit and utility facilities are also underway.

More than 3,400 people and over 600 units of special equipment are currently involved in construction. The project has reached 6 million hours worked without lost-time injuries.

"Particular attention is being paid to increasing local content in the implementation of the project. To date, contracts worth $1.205 billion have been signed with Kazakh companies. They are involved at all stages, from engineering and the production of equipment and materials to construction and installation works," KMG said.

During a meeting on major oil and gas chemical projects, Khassenov also reviewed a report on the construction of the Gas Separation Complex (GSC) at the Tengiz field and the main ethane and propane pipelines, which will supply feedstock to future petrochemical facilities.

The GSC project is more than 23% complete, with 17,344 piles already installed. More than 2,800 people are currently involved in its construction, over 77% of whom are residents of the Atyrau region.

World.title: Wildlife photos from around the world dazzle in competition
World.content:
A damsel fly peeking out of a window in a leaf has taken out the top prize in an ecology journal's annual photo competition.

Other images highlighted in the competition featured frogs, fish, birds, and ecologists hard at work — often in uncomfortable conditions.

The BMC Ecology and Evolution and BMC Zoology image competition is open to researchers in ecology, evolutionary biology, palaeontology and zoology from around the world.

This year, the winning entry came from Sritam Kumar Sethy, a student at Berhampur University in India, while Australian researchers and wildlife snagged awards in several categories.

Mr Kumar Sethy's photo (above) showed an orange-tailed marsh dart damsel fly (Ceriagrion cerinorubellum) in a wetland in the Indian state of Odisha.

Florida manatees drinking from a freshwater source in the Everglades National Park, USA. (Supplied: Brandon Güell, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

This image of manatees by Brandon Güellwas highly commended.

Relationships in nature

Victor Huertas Martin, a marine biologist at James Cook University, won the Relationship category with a photo of duelling giant cuttlefish (Ascarosepion apama) in the Spencer Gulf.

A male giant cuttlefish blocks the approach of another towards a female during the species’ annual spawning. (Supplied: Victor Huertas, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

He snapped a moment from the cuttlefish's famous annual breeding season, when tens of thousands of colour-changing fish gather in the shallow waters around Whyalla and squabble for mates.

Dr Huertas, who studies tropical fish, said he made the trip down to the cold South Australian waters out of interest.

"I was absolutely blown away by what I saw there," he said.

" The only thing that got me out of the water was the temperature. "

Dr Huertas said the giant cuttlefish were less shy than the tropical reef fish he was used to observing.

"They didn't seem to be bothered with my presence at all," he said.

"When they're busy mating, there's only one thing in mind, and they don't care about anything else."

Dr Huertas's trip was in 2023. This year, the waters around Whyalla have been eerily silent, with experts fearing the algal bloom has caused a crash in the cuttlefish population.

"I'm not only concerned about this population, but also the ramifications for the entire ecosystem," Dr Huertas said.

Dr Huertas said we do not yet know the extent of the damage to the cuttlefish population, or whether it will recover in the coming years.

" We're all holding our breath and hoping for the best. "

Noisy friarbirds mobbing a brown goshawk in the ACT's Mulligans Flat Woodland Sanctuary. (Supplied: Alwin Hardenbol, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

Alwin Hardenbol, a postdoctoral researcher at the Natural Resources Institute Finland, came runner-up in the category with a shot from Mulligans Flat in the ACT.

Dr Hardenbol, who studies forestry, said he was walking in the reserve "simply as a tourist" when he saw a showdown between a brown goshawk (Tachyspiza fasciata) and two noisy friarbirds (Philemon corniculatus).

The friarbirds were "mobbing" the predator: harassing, swooping and calling to discourage it and alert other birds in the area.

"Taking on a raptor as a much smaller bird must take quite some courage," Dr Hardenbol said.

While Dr Hardenbol has spent decades photographing nature, he said this shot was something of a lucky moment.

" But spending time in nature will often reward you like that. "

Protecting our planet

The winning image in the Protecting Our Planet category displayed a road linking islands along the St Lawrence Seaway, which connects North America's Great Lakes and the Atlantic Ocean.

This stereographic drone shot of the St Lawrence Seaway in North America won the Protecting Our Planet category. (Supplied: Allen Tian, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

The islands, which were made when a dam flooded the surrounding region in the 1950s, are now a bird sanctuary where photographer Allen Tian was conducting DNA research.

The runner-up photo in the category came from India's west coast, where locals have been helping olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings (Lepidochelys olivacea) make it safely into the ocean as part of a community-led conservation effort.

Runner-up in the Protecting Our Planet category, this picture shows a hatchling olive ridley sea turtle being helped into the surf by a local. (Supplied: Abhijeet Bayani, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

Research in action

The competition's overall runner-up showed a rainy night with students Alyson Yates and Ally Rounds attaching a radio transmitter to a northern red-legged frog (Rana aurora) to learn about its movements.

Competition runner-up shows students performing frog research near Portland, Oregon, USA. (Supplied: Ryan Wagner, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

Meanwhile, the Research In Action category winner depicted another dark, wet night, with undergraduate students sorting through a beach seine net sampling the coastal waters of New Brunswick, Canada.

The Research In Action category winner shows undergraduate students on a moonlit Canadian beach. (Supplied: Liam Brennan, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

Luke Jeffrey, a research fellow at Southern Cross University, was highly commended overall for his picture of himself in a Northern Territory melaleuca wetland.

Dr Jeffrey investigates microbes in tree bark, which can play a key role in greenhouse gas recycling.

Luke Jeffrey's selfie while climbing a tree in the Northern Territory to monitor microbial communities in its bark. (Supplied: Luke Jeffrey, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

Wildlife scientist Vineet Kumar's photo of a Himalayan cave was also highly commended overall.

Dr Kumar and a team of researchers from the Zoological Survey of India were in the area searching for an endangered Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus).

This image of a researcher resting in a Himalayan cave while on a bear hunt was highly commended. (Supplied: Vineet Kumar, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

The team, which researches interactions between bears and humans, was surprised to find the bearless cave had been used by nomadic shepherds grazing sheep.

An image of field technicians sampling wildlife in the Everglades was runner-up in the research in action category.

The runner-up in the Research In Action category displayed field technicians in Florida's Everglades National Park, USA. (Supplied: Brandon Güell, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

A full explanation of each image and the judgements has been published in a journal editorial.

World.title: North Korea fires missiles into sea as South Korea, US hold military drills
World.content:
North Korea has fired several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea, according to South Korea's military, a day after Seoul announced it was scaling back its military drills with the United States.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff said about 10 short-range ballistic missiles were launched from Pyongyang towards North Korea's eastern waters at around 5pm local time on Thursday.

South Korea's presidential national security council held an emergency meeting following the missile launches and issued a statement urging North Korea to halt ballistic missile launches that are banned by UN Security Council resolutions.

South Korea has since bolstered its surveillance posture and said it was closely coordinating information with the United States and Japan.

The Japanese prime minister's office also confirmed it had detected a suspected missile launch.

South Korea has reduced its training drills with the United States from 11 days to five. (AP: Ahn Young-joon)

The missile launch comes amid the US and South Korea's annual military training drills and less than a day after US President Donald Trump said he planned to meet North Korea leader Kim Jong Un later this year.

Trump says he will meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un later this year The US president made the announcement days after ordering the US scale back its military drills with South Korea.

The training drills will end six days early this year after Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back the exercise.

The Ulchi Freedom Shield is one of the main military exercises conducted by the US and South Korea each year to enhance their ability to cope with potential North Korean aggression.

While Washington and Seoul say their drills are defensive in nature, North Korea calls them an invasion rehearsal and often reacts with weapons tests.

Before this month's drills started, North Korea accused the US and South Korea of plotting more provocative exercises this summer and vowed to respond with "a new level of a deterrent".

China weighs in on Korean Peninsula tensions

South Korean National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac meets with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Seoul. (Yonhap via Reuters)

Thursday's missile launch also came as China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited South Korea.

During the visit, the foreign minister urged South Korea not to take sides between Beijing and Washington, saying the US should abandon its "hostile" policy towards North Korea to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

"The fundamental solution to the tensions on the Korean Peninsula lies in addressing the root causes of the problem and urging the United States to abandon its hostile policy toward North Korea," he said, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, during a meeting with South Korea's National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac.

China hopes South Korea will "achieve genuine strategic autonomy, refrain from bloc confrontation and taking sides, and develop relations with major powers including China and the United States in parallel and without contradiction".

North Korea also fired a short-range ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan earlier this month, a day after Pyongyang criticised Japan's military build-up in the region.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Russian missile strikes kill 13 in Kyiv, more than 30 injured
World.content:
Russian ballistic missiles have killed at least 13 people and injured more than 30 in Kyiv, authorities say, damaging buildings and severing power supply to some parts of the Ukrainian capital.

A fire broke out, and the upper floors of a nine-storey residential block were destroyed in the city's Solomianskyi district, where seven people were killed, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, calling for Friday to be observed as a day of mourning.

Two other districts also suffered damage, Mr Klitschko said on the Telegram messaging app, with non-residential facilities, warehouses, a school and a children's hospital hit.

Power company DTEK said it restored electricity to more than half of the roughly 90,000 homes left without power in the capital following the attack.

Russia has intensified its air strikes on Ukraine over the summer. (Reuters: Anatolii Stepanov)

"There used to be a building here, and now it's gone," said 45-year-old resident Maria Abramova.

She had only just reached her children's room after the air raid alert sounded when explosions rang out, blowing her windows out and "nearly killing" her husband.

Russia has stepped up air strikes on Ukraine in recent months, trying to exploit its smaller neighbour's critical shortage of interceptors to down ballistic missiles.

The Russian defence ministry said Moscow attacked Kyiv and the surrounding region with air strikes and drones, hitting facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub, as well as other targets.

A woman in Kyiv reacts after finding out her grandson has died in the Russian attacks. (Reuters: Anatolii Stepanov)

A resident reported hearing more than a dozen explosions. In the region around the Ukrainian capital, another person was killed, an official said on Telegram.

Ukraine's emergency service showed video of servicemen battling a blaze in a building and helping people to escape facilities destroyed during the night in Kyiv.

Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

Smoke rises from a food warehouse hit by a Russian missile strike near Kyiv. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Diplomatic efforts have failed so far to yield a lasting ceasefire in the war, which started with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Russian bank fires economist Andrei Klepach, one of Russia's most prominent macroeconomists, has predicted a social crisis and says costs are "mounting" over the Ukraine war.

A drone crashed into NATO and European Union member Romania during the Russian attack on Ukraine, the Romanian defence ministry said on Thursday. A drone also crossed Moldova's airspace, the country's military said.

Ukraine had handed proposals to US negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, for a plan to end the war, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said this month, and he has also repeatedly asked for interceptor missiles to ward off missile attacks.

Russia did not receive specific proposals for possible new meetings with US negotiators, foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the Izvestia newspaper.

But she added that Moscow would be ready to arrange a meeting at short notice.

Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner were last in Moscow last January and have not yet visited Kyiv.

Wires/ABC

World.title: 'Is this accurate?' How one note magnified the tragedy of bushwalker's family
World.content:
"Is this accurate?"

That was the immediate reaction of New South Wales Premier Chris Minns when he was passed a note in parliament shortly before midday.

He had already faced two hours of questioning in a budget estimates hearing and still had another hour to go.

The note was a surprising, but welcome distraction from questions about uranium mining.

After being assured the information was credible, the premier made an announcement that brought joy to the room.

"We've got some fantastic news, Mr Chair," he said.

"Lily Hooper has been found alive."

The NSW premier was handed the note during budget estimates. (ABC News)

There were murmurs of relief from MPs, many of whom had been following the news about the missing 18-year-old hiker.

Ms Hooper left her home south-west of Sydney on the morning of Wednesday, August 12, to go hiking in the Nattai National Park.

Her car was later found near the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, sparking a large-scale multi-agency search involving nearly 1,000 people, according to police.

The premier went on to thank the police, the State Emergency Service (SES), defence personnel and the many others who had joined the search.

It was a moment of levity in a sometimes combative hearing.

The premier's announcement was widely reported, including by the ABC.

About 25 minutes later, the premier was handed another note, containing the worst possible news.

A tragic miscommunication

Lily Hooper's body was found after an eight-day search. (Supplied: NSW Police)

By that stage, the hearing had resumed normal programming, with opposition MP Natalie Ward asking a series of pointed questions about the office of local government.

After conferring with Secretary of the Cabinet Office, Kate Boyd, a stony-faced Mr Minns made another announcement.

"I've got some terrible news," he said.

"I apologise to the committee, but it seems as if the early advice was wrong.

"Lily's body's been found, and she's been found deceased."

"Oh my god," replied committee chair Jeremy Buckingham.

Members of the Australia Defence Force also joined the search. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The premier continued.

"I only raise that because I made the earlier advice and I'm very sorry for that," he said.

"This is obviously devastating, and I'm just profoundly sad for her family and all those concerned."

Police said about 11:30am a body believed to be that of Ms Hooper was located in bushland.

The premier's anguish was plain to see.

Not only had he been provided with incorrect information, but his earlier statement had brought the community an immense sense of relief that was abruptly snatched away.

People would be entitled to wonder how such an error could be made.

It soon became clear the miscommunication occurred much further down the chain.

Unfortunately, it made its way to the top before anyone could stop it.

The error fuelled by 'elation'

The NSW assistant police commissioner said there was a delay in effectively communicating the fact that Lily Hooper had died. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Speaking to reporters in the Southern Highlands, NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Joseph Cassar pointed to the communication challenges search teams were facing using handheld radios.

An SES volunteer made the initial discovery and was following protocol by reporting it up, he said.

However, he said there was a delay in effectively communicating the fact that Ms Hooper had died.

During the intervening period of between eight and 10 minutes, Ms Hooper's family, who were in close contact with the police, were led to believe she was alive.

Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon apologised "unreservedly" to the family.

"The miscommunication obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found, and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved," he said.

"Certainly, those at the command post were elated.

"Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously we know now the impact on her family."

By that stage, the initial report of Ms Hooper having been found had already found its way to the government.

Police have well-established lines of communication into the offices of both the premier and the police minister, Yasmin Catley.

Word travels fast, by necessity.

During media conferences or Question Time, both are regularly asked for updates on police investigations or emergency operations, so they need to be well-briefed.

A large-scale multi-agency search was launched. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Just as the public is right to expect that the information the premier provides is accurate, he is right to expect the information being passed up the chain is correct.

The commissioner said the incorrect report was passed via police commands into the offices of both the premier and the police minister.

While he "wasn't given notice" of the premier's announcement, he was not surprised that he had made it.

"When Lily was located, obviously there was elation," Commissioner Lanyon said.

"That information got passed through very quickly.

"It's unsurprising that it went quickly up into government."

Police have now committed to reviewing and improving their communication on the ground, particularly when working with the SES.

It is also likely to prompt some rebalancing between the speed and accuracy of the information they provide to the government, which today showed how quickly it can disseminate it.

On this occasion, that balance was off, magnifying both a mistake and a family's tragedy.

World.title: 'Completely unacceptable': Albanese lashes AFL over response to Swans scandal
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised the AFL over its handling of the current scandal engulfing the league.

On Wednesday, the Swans stood down five players for the rest of the AFL season — vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey — for breaching club standards for drinking and bringing women to the hotel.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad have since flown to New South Wales and are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Swans players James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey and Riley Bice have been stood down. (Getty Images/ABC News)

Mr Albanese told 7.30 that he felt the initial response was not good enough.

"It's extraordinary that this has occurred," Mr Albanese said.

"The idea that this is occurring is completely untenable, and the initial response as well was, I think, completely unacceptable.

"The NRL have a no-fault stand down clause for issues like this, but the first thoughts should have been always about women and their safety.

" I don't think that occurred at this time. The AFL certainly needs to do better. "

That initial response came on Monday afternoon when Swans CEO and Fremantle Dockers great Matthew Pavlich confirmed several players had been linked to the alleged incident.

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich has issued several statements this week. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," Mr Pavlich said on Monday.

"But safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation."

On Tuesday AFL CEO Andrew Dillon described the allegations as "deeply disturbing" in a statement.

On Thursday night the ABC reported that detectives investigating have been told some players paid female adult entertainers to consume drugs off their bodies.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mr Albanese said the AFL and the Swans should "have a good look" at their culture.

Albanese to press Israel over Frankcom

While Mr Albanese was focused on several issues at home, the major geopolitical issue of the day involved Israel.

On Wednesday night, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing over a 2024 strike on a humanitarian convoy, which killed Australian woman Zomi Frankcom.

Ms Frankcom was killed in a strike by the IDF. (Supplied: Facebook)

The decision was described as an "outrage" by Foreign Minister Penny Wong on Thursday morning.

Mr Albanese told 7.30 he wanted a much more transparent response from the Israeli government.

"It clearly is an outrage and there's a need for a far more transparent and clear explanation from the Israeli government other than what we've received," Mr Albanese said.

Asked if that would involve an independent investigation, Mr Albanese said it was one option.

"It's certainly not good enough that on World Humanitarian Day ... they release this so-called report that essentially says, 'Yes, we're responsible, but nothing to see here', he said".

"Zomi represented the best of Australians out there in a dangerous area, helping her fellow global citizens as she had in other parts of the world that were suffering conflict as well. And that's why it deserves better.

"Her family deserved better, and frankly, Australia deserves better.

"We will press the Israeli government.

"[We] will discuss with Ms Frankcom's family. They deserve to be consulted on these issues and we'll do that, and then we'll make an announcement in coming days."

PM concedes podcast appearance was 'an error'

The Prime Minister was also asked about criticism he's faced over several comments he made on the Deep Bush podcast.

Loading...

Mr Albanese first came under scrutiny for playing "shag, marry, date" on the podcast, which was broadcast in July.

He has since unequivocally apologised for saying he would "shag" Kylie Minogue.

Recently it was hand gestures he made on the podcast, while referring to a pair of melons given to him by Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, that caused controversy.

Mr Albanese has not apologised specifically for the melon interaction and maintains that the gestures have been misinterpreted.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

However, he told 7.30 that in hindsight he should not have gone on the podcast and that he had learned from it.

"I learned that I need to do better every day," Mr Albanese said.

"If I had my time again ... then I wouldn't have done that podcast.

" We have a view which is trying to talk to as many people as possible, but clearly that was an error. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Zomi Frankcom's family 'deeply disappointed' IDF won't pursue charges
World.content:
The family of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, who was killed in an Israeli strike while delivering humanitarian aid in Gaza in 2024, has slammed the Israeli military's decision not to pursue criminal charges against the commanders who ordered the attack.

The statement, issued by Zomi's brother Mal on behalf of the Frankcom family, said family members were "deeply disappointed" by the decision, having spent the past two years waiting for justice while "hoping and calling for an independent criminal investigation".

"Zomi and her colleagues deserve more than an internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing," they said.

" The families of the victims deserve transparency and an independent judicial assessment of the criminal responsibility for the international humanitarian law violations that took place on that day. "

Ms Frankcom was one of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers killed on April 1, 2024, while taking part in a convoy helping to deliver food and other supplies to northern Gaza.

The group was travelling in three armoured cars branded with the World Central Kitchen logo, and driving through part of the Gaza Strip that had been declared a "humanitarian fire control zone" while coordinating movements with the IDF (Israel Defense Forces).

An Israeli drone fired three missiles at the convoy — one at each of the cars in succession — as survivors of the initial strike attempted to move from one vehicle to another.

Wreckage of one of three World Central Kitchen vehicles destroyed in the strikes. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

An Australian investigation into the Israeli government's response to the incident, led by retired defence chief Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin, found the deaths had been the result of the first vehicle being misidentified due to a number of factors, including the presence of armed security in the vicinity, confirmation bias and a "failure within the IDF to fully disseminate and/or read the detailed movement plan approved by the convoy".

Wong declares 'difficult time' in relations with Israel Foreign Minister Penny Wong says she has "no confidence" in the IDF investigation that cleared Israeli soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.

The subsequent strikes were also found to be a breach of IDF procedures and the rules of engagement, echoing the findings of a rapid FFAM ("fact-finding and assessment mechanism") investigation conducted by the IDF in the days following the incident.

Two IDF officers were fired in the weeks after the strikes, while others were reprimanded.

In their statement released on Thursday evening, Ms Frankcom's family expressed disagreement with the finding that there was no wrongdoing involved that merited at least a criminal investigation, highlighting the follow-up strikes as well as the fact that one of the officers involved had reportedly signed a letter earlier that year calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.

They also expressed outrage at the timing of the announcement, which came on World Humanitarian Day, an internationally recognised day dedicated to those who have died working for humanitarian causes.

A humanitarian award has since been created in Ms Frankcom's name. (Supplied: X)

The family had been standing alongside Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong at an event at Parliament House just hours prior to the announcement, launching a humanitarian award in Ms Frankcom's name.

"For it to be announced on World Humanitarian Day, the day the world pauses to remember those who have lost their lives while helping others … is an insult to my sister's memory," Ms Frankcom's brother Mal said.

Senator Wong similarly expressed anger at the announcement, saying she had no confidence in the IDF's findings, and calling in Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, to explain the decision.

Calling today's events a "difficult time" in diplomatic relations with Israel, she said she was informed of the IDF's decision just minutes before it was publicly announced, and did not have time to alert Ms Frankcom's family.

World.title: Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning
World.content:
The Penrith Panthers have held on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

The Panthers shot out to a 22-0 lead courtesy of a Brian To'o hat-trick and Liam Henry try, but did not score again after the half-hour mark.

Back rower Liam Martin was sent to the sin-bin for a professional foul shortly before half-time and Penrith was Lindsay Smith was binned just after the break for repeated ruck infringements.

Melbourne managed to get on the board against 11 men when Tyran Wishart skipped through the teeth of the defence, and Jack Howarth put a move on Izack Tago to crash over soon after Smith returned to the field.

Jack Cogger joined the list of sin-binned players, which also included Storm back rower Oryn Keeley from the first half, when he hit Wishart high, leading to Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown's try on the right wing.

But wayward kicking by Nick Meaney and some attacking miscues kept the Storm from getting too close as they fell out of the finals race for the first time since 2010, when they played for no points due to salary cap infringements.

Prior to that, the Storm have not missed the finals since 2002, before Craig Bellamy took over as coach.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Holman stars on farewell as Suns out-muscle Saints to begin Round 24
World.content:
Retiring Gold Coast hero Nick Holman kicked two goals as his side finished its season with a 23-point win at Docklands.

The Suns led at every change, beginning with a seven-goal opening term before running out winners by 14.19 (103) to 12.8 (80).

Ben King kicked three goals in what is likely his final game for Gold Coast, while Leo Lombard also had three and Holman two.

Hugh Boxshall kicked three for the Saints while Liam Ryan, Mitch Owens and Ryan Byrnes had two each.

Both the Suns and Saints were playing for pride with both sides missing the finals.

Gold Coast skipper Noah Anderson told Seven it had been a "difficult year", and that the team needed a week or two "to reflect on how we can grow."

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Perth dad dies after allegedly being attacked by ‘group of Aussies’ in a Bali bar
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth dad dies after allegedly being attacked by ‘group of Aussies’ in a Bali bar Rebecca Peppiatt and Amber Wilkinson August 20, 2026 — 9:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth father has died after allegedly being attacked by a group of Australians while on holiday in Bali. Paul Dougan, from Gosnells, underwent three surgeries, including to have his spleen removed, after the attack 10 days ago. Paul Dougan has died after allegedly being set upon by a group of Aussies in a Bali bar 10 days ago. He was on a trip with friends when he was allegedly assaulted at One Tribe bar in Kuta by a group of strangers, believed to be Australian, after his friends had left to go home. “To have this happen to him, of all people, is just devastating,” friend David Coughtrie told 9News Perth.



“He’s not the kind of guy to go looking for that sort of trouble. “He’d grabbed his partner and said, ‘Let’s get out of here’. As he stood up he was confronted by a person that said, ‘What did you say?’ and pretty much didn’t wait for an answer and just struck him.” Perth father Paul Dougan has been hospitalised in Bali after allegedly being assaulted by fellow Australians while on holiday. GoFundMe Dougan’s injuries included 10 broken ribs and severe internal bleeding. His family rushed to Bali to be with him and on Wednesday his son Liam launched a GoFundMe page to help pay for mounting medical costs.



But as donations started pouring in, Dougan lost his battle while in intensive care. Related Article Inquest Behind bars for 30 years, out for 79 days: Perth inquest probes complex final months of a killer Liam posted to social media saying, “it wasn’t meant to be this way Dad”, adding, “I will love and remember you for the rest of my life and I will continue to make you proud. “I am shattered, lost, heartbroken and confused but grateful I ever got to call you my Dad,” the post, made on Thursday evening, read. Liam had earlier made a video explaining what had happened and how Indonesian police were in the process of trying to track down those responsible.



“It looks to be a group of four of the suspects that we’ve got and [they were] beating him heavily while on the floor,” he said. On the fundraising page, Liam wrote his father was “brutally assaulted by a group of Australians who are yet to be identified”. “They beat and kicked him multiple times putting him in a life-threatening condition,” it read. “From this Paul suffered internal bleeding and 10 broken ribs, has undergone three major surgeries, had his spleen removed, required four blood transfusions, and currently has drains in both his lungs and abdomen as a result of the internal injuries and bleeding from the attack. “He has now been in ICU for 10 days and remains sedated following his third surgery.”



On Thursday evening the fundraiser had received more than $45,000 in donations. With 9News Perth

World.title: Swill waters run deep
World.content:
“Apropos David Sayers’ soft drink saga (C8), in my teens, I worked at the local lolly water factory in Muswellbrook in the holidays,” writes Denis Cartledge of Tenterfield. “It was a Friday afternoon event for one particular worker to be thrown in the softwater tank that supplied the factory. He rarely washed, and his workmates thought they’d help his cleanliness regime. Looking back, I don’t think the tank was drained, cleaned and/or refilled. It was around that time we decided to stop buying a mixed crate of lolly water every few months.”

The current dress code discussion (C8) is revealing a few workarounds. Here’s Bev Matthews of Wallerawang: “Back in the early ’80s, three friends and I tried to get into a club in Parramatta. One of the boys had a collarless shirt on, and they wouldn’t let him in. I happened to be wearing a knitted cardigan with a collar (like I said, it was the ’80s). He donned it, and voilà, they let him in.”

“In the late 1970s, my brother-in-law went for an after work beer at the Manly Yacht Club in Brisbane, of which he was a member,” says Colleen Riga of Potts Point. “Clad in his work gear consisting of boots, stubbies and polo shirt, he was told that club rules required a tie for evening entry. They had no problem with the work gear, so, looking through a box under the counter containing ‘emergency neckwear’ they presented him with a clip-on bow-tie (or ‘blowfly’ as he incorrectly heard) and he was free to enjoy a coldie.”

Reading about Mash McDonald’s in Iran (C8) reminded Ann MacKenzie of St Ives of the time she was in Tehran in 2017 and noticed a fast food establishment dubbed ZFC.

In reply to Stephen Tait’s inquiry into the wellbeing of Dirranbandi pubsters the Norton Brothers (C8), Janice Creenaune of Austinmer says the visit was earlier in the year, on Anzac Day in fact, and that the pub was “heaving with 2-up patrons. However, today we are off to camp near the ‘Hog and Billy’ in Girilambone, (known colloquially as ‘Girl’ I believe). Is there anybody we can look up for you there, Stephen?”

World.title: Inching towards a more prosperous time
World.content:
There are small beams of light peeping through for the economy, but don't get excited about a recovery just yet. It's uneven, and not for everyone.

Inching towards a more prosperous time The Detail Download MP3 24m

Tourists are coming back, manufacturing is picking up, our primary industries are doing well and that's filtering into South Island cities. We're seeing some good company results, inflation is down and the services sector is finally seeing some growth.

We should see economic expansion in the third and fourth quarters this year.

That's the good news.

The bad news is, improvement is slight and sometimes marginal; unemployment, especially youth unemployment, is still high; America's erratic leadership and war in the Middle East continues to create uncertainty; Auckland is dragging its feet; small business liquidations are at record numbers; there's political uncertainty and we could be in for a long, very dry summer.

And not everyone will be caught in the uplift. The South Island is well ahead of the North, and a large sector of the population is still struggling with the cost of living.

Today on The Detail we look at where there are encouraging signs and where the uncertainty remains, plus the tiny Central Otago town of Naseby and how it's feeding into, and off of, this pickup in the economy - trading in on its natural beauty and a tourist taste for adventure.

The economic data is coming thick and fast. For example, tourism, our second biggest export earner, saw 3.6 million overseas visitor arrivals in the year to June - 300,000 more than last year. We've seen an all-time record for Australians visiting, and a big increase in Chinese tourists.

One of the more interesting figures is how much ready-mixed concrete was poured - a million cubic metres in the June quarter, up 12 percent on the same time last year.

Andrew Kelleher, the executive director of financial services company Shaw and Partners, jokes that he always looks forward to getting that figure.

"It's sort of the foundation for most building projects, isn't it? You don't build unless you've got some concrete in there somewhere."

The figure is the solid evidence that building consents are translating into actual work.

But the figures also show a clear difference between north and south.

"This is so evident in almost all of the data that we see, the housing market is the most stark illustration of it ... where you've seen very different experiences in these markets from the two big urban areas of Auckland and Wellington versus what's happening in the South Island.

"A lot of this is to do with what I call proximity to primary produce markets. Somewhere like the Canterbury region and Christchurch itself, it's very close to what's happening in dairy, whereas you go to Auckland, you go to Wellington ... Wellington you have a lot of government sector there, Auckland much more services and manufacturing based and you're just seeing completely different outcomes in these two places.

"So it's very much a two-speed and a bifurcation of what's going on."

He says normally when New Zealand's done well economically there's a combination of three factors behind it - a house price boom, increasing numbers of people coming into the country, and a government spending splurge.

"You could argue that we certainly haven't got two of them right now - we haven't got the house prices booming, and we're not importing lots of people. And then we could probably have ongoing debates, robust debates ... about what is the actual level of government spending because it hasn't actually dropped very much since the coalition government has been in power.

"If we can get a recovery that isn't dependent on simply speculation in the housing market and house prices rising, that's a good thing."

It means first home buyers have more access to the market, which is a positive, but it does take away the feel-good factor from people whose real estate is getting more valuable, who might otherwise be out, happy to spend money.

"But if we're building a more productive economy, and if we're building an economy based not on speculation but based on doing some real stuff, that's probably a good thing but I don't know if we're going to see it be quite as frothy as it might be, and certainly not felt as universally as if it was based on house prices going up."

Kelleher says there are still real pockets out there where people won't feel the effect of improvement, "and this becomes quite topical given we've got an election in November".

"We're running out of time for that sort of feel-good factor of economic growth to actually reach into households around New Zealand."

Alan MacDonald, the head of advocacy and strategy at the Employers and Manufacturers Association, says all the conversation about manufacturing improvement has concentrated on what's been driven by the primary sector in the regions, but the figures also tell a bit of "an underplayed story".

"If you look at the Performance and Manufacturing Index, that's had quite a good run over the last 12 months or so. It's a good solid data set and it tells a pretty reasonable story at the moment that underpins that recovery piece."

Food production is always a factor, "but we do some really smart stuff, some of the stuff we do around composites and things like that, the stuff that goes into rockets for Rocket Lab and it goes into Formula 1 cars, the big racing yachts and that sort of stuff. It's not unique to us but it's something we're very good at.

"We're also good at a whole lot of niche engineering things, so you go around some of the warehouses and things that our members typically hang out in and they're doing some great stuff. For example laser-guided mowing systems ... who does that? Well actually there's a company down in the Bay of Plenty that does that, and they export it, and they're mowing 80 or so golf courses in the US."

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: How lessons from the Covid-19 pandemic could be applied to current flu outbreak
World.content:
A professor of public health hopes lessons from the Covid-19 pandemic can be used in the current flu outbreak.

Auckland has had its worst week for flu hospitalisations in a decade, with 177 people admited to the region's four public hospitals, while New Zealand is also close to the highest influenza rate in four years.

University of Otago professor Michael Baker said the late season surge was putting a huge strain on health services.

He said while there was little appetite for the "extraordinary measures" used during the pandemic, the insights gained from that time could be applied to the flu.

Some clinicians were already drawing on Covid-era practices to deal with the current flu surge, he said, such as separating patients with respiratory symptoms.

Baker said the clearly understood Covid-19 alert system - which linked increasing infection risk to stronger measures - had value for seasonal respiratory infections.

"At a baseline level, this approach could mean the usual measures of vaccination and staying home when unwell.

"As respiratory infection activity increases, additional measures could be considered, for example, mask use in healthcare and other higher-risk settings such as waiting rooms and public transport, and additional protections for particularly vulnerable groups, including people in aged residential care," he said."

Baker said the framework could provide a routine way of communicating to the public the risk of a range of illnesses and the appropriate response.

He said New Zealanders were already used to such a system to communicate changing risks from weather, fire danger and other hazards.

"The current influenza surge raises an important question: should we also have an ongoing, nationally understood respiratory-infection risk framework that tells people when the risk is low, when it is increasing, and what they can do to reduce transmission and protect themselves and those who are most vulnerable?"

Fears outbreak could exceed 2022 peak

There are fears the current rapid outbreak of flu cases could exceed the peak year of 2022 in the next few weeks.

Canterbury University disease modelling expert Michael Plank. Supplied.

A disease modelling expert from Canterbury University, Michael Plank, said soaring cases would likely hit a peak in the next couple of weeks.

These were likely to rise higher than the post-pandemic rebound four years ago, he said, before tapering off in spring. In 2022, PHF Science data showed a flu rate of 27.4 per 100,000 population. For the week ending 16 August, 2026, the rate was 15.39 and rising, with 177 hospital admissions.

Plank said there was a late wave of influenza last year, when the new varient cropped up in around August and September. He said it meant the illness was still present in spring and early summer, when normally it would disappear in September or early October.

"Possibly that late flu wave last year has meant we've had a delayed start to this season, but certainly it's really taken off in the last few weeks and we're seeing very high levels of influenza now."

Plank said it wasn't too late to vaccinate against the flu and that this year's vaccince was well-matched with the current flu strain.

World.title: More job cuts on the cards at Conservation Department, union says
World.content:
The union for public servants says more cuts are on the table at the Department of Conservation.

The Public Service Association said a proposed restructure of the communications team could see 28 roles axed.

RNZ understands staff are very upset by the proposal, which includes the disestablishment of the entire media and communications unit.

The union said 33 positions were proposed to be disestablished within the communications team and 37 new positions created.

Under the proposal, 25 fixed-term positions would naturally come to an end and three new fixed-term roles would be established, it said.

"In total, the team would be reduced from 83 roles to 55," the union said.

The Department of Conservation (DOC) did not confirm those numbers.

DOC director of strategic communications and engagement Fiona Weightman said proposed changes to how the communications team is organised had been put to staff.

She said no decisions had been made.

World.title: Don't underestimate machinery, coroner says, after arborist caught on stump grinder
World.content:
The death of an arborist caught on a stump grinder is a stark reminder not to underestimate machinery, a coroner says.

Groundsperson Kevin Barry, 69, had been contracted to remove two tree stumps on a grass berm in Whangārei on the 15th of April 2025, but was later found laying on the ground by a member of the public with critical head injuries.

He was taken to Whangārei Hospital but his injuries were unsurvivable.

A post-mortem examination found he had suffered severe lacerations to his brain.

Barry's death was investigated by WorkSafe, which determined his sleeve had been caught on the stump grinder, pulling him towards the blade.

Coroner Ian Telford summarised the likely sequence of events.

Coroner Ian Telford. Pool / Chris Skelton / Stuff

"After the stump grinding was completed, Mr Barry raised the cutting arm so that the cutter wheel was clear of the ground and the surrounding wood chips," he wrote.

"Contrary to the required operating procedure, the cutter wheel was not disengaged after the stump removal had been completed. It instead remained spinning."

Telford said the grinder was moved at an angle facing the edge of the footpath towards Barry's car.

"For reasons unknown, possibly while attempting to pass between the stump grinder and the parked vehicle, Mr Barry approached the area of the spinning cutter wheel," he continued.

"This placed Mr Barry within the danger zone and resulted in the spinning cutter wheel catching the right arm of Mr Barry's long-sleeve top and pulling him into the cutter wheel at such a speed that he was unable to activate the emergency stop on the remote-control unit before being incapacitated."

The director of the company Barry worked for told police he was "a very good operator, careful, and safety conscious", and the coroner noted that Barry was wearing appropriate PPE, had been thoroughly trained and knew the machine well.

WorkSafe's investigation found no health and safety breaches.

"I am satisfied that Mr Barry was acutely aware of these hazards and was a careful and safety-conscious operator who was regarded as highly competent," Telford wrote.

"Nevertheless, this tragic accident is a reminder that, even in the hands of skilled operators, the risks associated with this machinery remain significant and ever-present."

He said the accident should serve as a stark reminder to others in the sector.

"The need for constant vigilance when working around exposed moving parts may seem obvious, but this accident is a stark reminder that the dangers posed by these machines must never be underestimated," he said.

World.title: No guarantee shelter can be provided for every rough sleeper - officials
World.content:
Weeks before the government is set to give police powers to move on rough sleepers, officials have admitted to RNZ they can't guarantee immediate shelter for anyone on any given night.

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson says she's grateful it's been "formally acknowledged", but is "deeply distressed" that's the reality in the country.

It comes as the largest provider of the most immediate form of shelter tells RNZ it's managing with the resources it has, but demand is "relentless".

In June, it was reported that Ministry of Social Development (MSD) managers had performance measures related to reducing emergency housing numbers. These measures have now been refocused to achieve "sustainable housing".

At the time, the prime minister admitted he did not know there was no night shelter in Auckland for people sleeping rough.

Since then, RNZ has attempted to understand what shelter is available for someone who is sleeping rough.

Over the past month, RNZ sought clarification from both MSD and the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) - which leads the government's overall programme of work to address rough sleeping - to understand where exactly someone is supposed to go if they need shelter immediately.

After multiple requests, RNZ was finally told by MCERT "there is no guarantee that shelter can be provided for every person in every circumstance in every location".

The agency said access to accommodation was dependent on a range of factors such as "an individual's circumstances, location, service capacity, and real-time availability of accommodation and appropriate support", all of which could change quickly it said.

Robinson told RNZ she'd never had it formally acknowledged there was no guarantee, "I am distressed and I am calling for change."

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson. Auckland City Mission

It comes as the government's move on orders legislation, which has received strong opposition, are being progressed ahead of the election.

The law would give police the power to order people as young as 14 to move elsewhere or face a possible jail sentence if they were being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping.

It also comes following reports of rough sleepers dying outdoors overnight, a man found unresponsive in a Cuba Street doorway in Wellington and a woman found unresponsive on New Brighton beach in Christchurch. RNZ understands another rough sleeper died in Auckland in July.

So for those who had nowhere else to go, and may be told to move on, where exactly could they go?

Understanding the current situation

As recently as Sunday, the minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith told TVNZ's Q+A there were "resources available and places available for people 24/7".

Emergency housing grants are the government's primary mechanism for providing immediate shelter to people who have "nowhere else to go" and "can't stay where they are".

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said in July emergency housing still existed "because there will always be people facing genuine housing crises".

"But now it's being used as it was always intended: as a temporary last resort."

Housing providers and social services have consistently said the governments tightened emergency housing criteria has resulted in an uptick in homelessness. That concern was raised by RNZ as early as March last year, with Community Housing Aotearoa chief executive Paul Gilberd saying again this week there was a direct link between the two.

The minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

As recently as Thursday, Serena Moran - a nurse practitioner and clinic lead at Te Aro Health Centre in Wellington - told RNZ there'd been an increase in rough sleepers she was treating, including people being released from prison with no plans to continue accessing antipsychotic medication.

She said the reality most days was treating patients who may have been assaulted and having nowhere to send them.

"I basically have to say to them, 'I'm sorry, I can't find you anywhere to stay tonight. You'll need to go back to the street. I'll give you pain relief. I'll try and make you feel as comfortable as I can'."

But ministers and MSD have consistently maintained that emergency housing remains available to anyone who meets the criteria and has a "genuine need".

Ministers and MSD have also repeatedly said that people who did not receive emergency housing could have their "needs met in another way", including through other housing pathways.

Other options include:

transitional housing;

social housing; and

immediate access transitional housing

But none of those pathways guaranteed a person sleeping rough today would have somewhere safe to sleep tonight, especially if the limited immediate access transitional housing beds were full. There were only 65 nationwide.

Kāhui Tū Kaha provided the majority of these beds and told RNZ it was managing with the resources it had, but said the demand was "relentless". It also accepted referrals from police and hospitals overnight.

On Thursday evening, it accepted an elderly woman with physical access needs and a 17-year-old who had both been sleeping on the street. It also accepted a woman becoming homeless due to family violence, and a young woman who police wanted separated from a violent partner.

Kāhui Tū Kaha said things were tight but "we're constantly juggling".

Housing minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What shelter is actually available tonight?

Over the past month, RNZ asked MSD and MCERT multiple times what options were available for someone sleeping on the streets to go somewhere that night - more specifically, to get a bed under a roof within 24 hours.

Through various responses and phone calls, RNZ received the following information.

RNZ was told that emergency housing "is not necessarily the best option for rough sleepers" who may have a range of complex needs and require additional support.

MSD noted there were more outreach and support services for rough sleepers announced in June by associate housing minister Tama Potaka, and referenced the additional $14.5 million attached.

"Of those who approach MSD for emergency housing, 89 percent receive either emergency housing, transitional housing, help with a private rental, or hardship assistance."

In response, RNZ asked for figures around the percentage of people who were declined emergency housing and offered "some other form of assistance", specifically actual shelter tonight - noting that someone could not sleep in a food grant, but an official information act request was required, which has since been made.

MSD also outlined that emergency housing was intended as a last resort - despite earlier stating it wasn't the "best option". Its service centre hours were between 8:30am to 5pm Monday to Friday and 9:30am to 5pm on Wednesdays.

It was possible for clients to receive a short-term grant outside of service hours, to "meet immediate housing needs until client can attend the next available appointment", but MSD wasn't able to provide the percentage of calls received outside hours and how many of those were granted without an official information act request, which has since been made.

Where possible MSD would refer people with an urgent housing need to suitable transitional housing or Housing First placements - these were funded by MCERT and generally provided more support than was available to someone in Emergency Housing.

Associate housing minister Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

MCERT's response clarified the different housing pathways for those in need:

Housing First

This supported people experiencing "chronic homelessness" to access and remain in stable housing. Support was available for as long as needed, but you had to have been sleeping rough for at least 12 months over the past three years to be considered. Those "new" to rough sleeping weren't elegible by definition.

The government announced an additional 300 homes for Housing First in 2025, following the concerns of increased homelessness.

Transitional housing

Transitional Housing offered "short-term, temporary accommodation" for those who may be affected by a change in circumstances. It also provided tailored support. Emergency referrals could generally be accomodated here.

However, MCERT confirmed the total number of contracted transitional housing places had fallen since 2023, that's despite increasing reliance on transitional housing as an alternative to emergency housing.

It said there were around 300 less places contracted in June 2026, compared to November 2023, reflecting the "planned exit of higher-cost motel-based places, as well as routine fluctuations associated with portfolio management", MCERT said.

As well, when existing transitional housing beds were redesignated as "immediate access" beds from December 2025, MCERT did not specify those beds were replaced elsewhere in the system.

Immediate access transitional housing

This is the most immediate option available, where contracted providers could accommodate eligible households without the need to first go through "standard MSD assessment and referral processes".

MCERT confirmed:

World.title: Big names back for All Blacks as team to play Springboks revealed
World.content:
The All Blacks have recalled several star players with Cam Roigard, Will Jordan and Damian McKenzie named to start in this weekend's test against the Springboks in Johannesburg.

The trio return from injury to take their place in the side while Ardie Savea resumes the captaincy duties after being rested for the first three games of the South African tour.

Savea is at No.8 with coach Dave Rennie retaining the loose forward trio from last month's win against Ireland, with Luke Jacobson at openside and Tupou Vaa'i at blindside.

Ardie Savea scores a try against Ireland. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Codie Taylor is at hooker with Tyrel Lomax and Ethan de Groot the starting props.

There was plenty of speculation as to who would play lock and Rennie has gone with Fabian Holland and Josh Lord in the second row, with Vaa'i to provide cover.

In the backs, Roigard returns at halfback with Ruben Love at first-five and Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield.

McKenzie has overcome the ankle injury that ruled him out of the win over the Bulls last weekend and will start at fullback, with Jordan and Josh Moorby on the wings.

Rennie has gone with a 5-3 split of forwards and backs on the bench, which includes front rowers Asafo Aumua, George Bower and Fletcher Newell, loose forwards Peter Lakai and Anton Segner, midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown, halfback Kyle Preston and outside back Leroy Carter.

Damian McKenzie celebrates a try with teammates. Photosport

Rennie said they can't wait to run out on Ellis Park on Sunday morning (NZT).

"After all the build up and anticipation, our whole touring squad is excited to get this first Test underway," Rennie said.

"We have selected a balanced mix of big match, experienced players and younger players who have earned the right to play in this first Test."

Rennie said the three games against the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls in South Africa have proved invaluable as they prepare for their biggest challenge of the year so far.

"The first three franchise games have exposed our newer players to the way South African teams play and have been fantastic in helping us build combinations and develop the game we want to play.

"We know the Test series will be a huge step up. We're well aware of what the Springboks will bring to the contest and the pressure that will come to bear. They are number one in the world, playing at their spiritual home in front of their passionate fans, so we will have to be at our very best on Saturday."

Josh Moorby in action against the Bulls. Photosport

Savea, Roigard and Jordan will make their first appearance of the tour in the match, while Savea and Taylor are playing their 110th Tests.

It will be Savea's 18th Test against South Africa and Taylor's 17th.

Segner and Moorby will be playing the Springboks for the first time.
